comments.text: I’m confused, when researching gpu’s, how many 4060’s are there, you’ve got msi ventus 2x, nvidia geforce rtx, then depending on what video you watch it can be msi nvidia geforce. Does nvidia distribute their tech to different brands or is it effectively all the same thing?
comments.author: @melódic_breeze_VIIIV

comments.text: Both, really. The actual GPU is a small chip just like a CPU. What other brands like MSI do is engineer the board that holds that chip and plugs into the PCIE slot, as well as the heatsink that cools it and the external shroud that holds the fans and RGB lights and other cosmetic things. That's how you get "the same" GPU with different fan counts or slot heights or low profile versions and so on. NVIDIA themselves create a version of all this as well, known as Founders Editions.

comments.text:
If you're still looking, the first thing to see is which component is causing the problem with task manager. If your CPU is maxing out but the GPU isn't, that is the culprit. But upgrading the CPU may also require upgrading your BIOS, or even the whole motherboard. It may also require an additional cooler.
If the GPU is maxing out first, which one are you running? [if you don't remember, win key > dxdiag > display]
Sometimes not having enough VRAM may also cause stutters.

As a general GPU suggestion, the 6600, 6600xt, and 6650xt are all really good value for a solid 1080/1440p experience if you only care about performance metrics and not power efficiency or software support/features.
You can find these under a bunch of different brands, but they're the same hardware. The 3 brands I would look for most are ASRock, XFX Speedster, and Gigabyte.

comments.text:
Being upset as a consumer is totally justified. It's not just nVidia as a tech manufacturer that abnormally increased prices over products that fall against expectations. 
Then again, I don't believe this rant is quite balanced. In terms of raw perfomance, the 6700xt competitor does a little bit better for the same price. Also, hardware specs are a bit boosted. 
It's important not to forget these aren't the only variables you should take into account. Switching to a brand new graphics card isn't always done independently. Upgrading your CPU, Mobo or PSU can also happen simultaneously depending on your configuration. So, keep in mind that RTX 4060 is only a 100W hungry graphics card that benefits from software boosters like DLSS and Frame Gen. 

Whichever you choose is a fine choice in my opinion. It all comes down to brand bias. Personally, I've always liked Nvidia & I'm not yet convinced AMD has done everything in their power to catch up.

The 4060 is a great card for my needs as its going to run my games at high/ultra settings at 1440p 60fps/114fps as well as been much more power efficient then other cards which is going to save me money on electricity compared to other cards.
I think these guys are been waaaay too harsh on it tbh.
If you want pure performance, then sure, theres better opitions, but to be honest for my needs I think this card is good for the price as it'll pay for itself in time with the money I'll save on electricity.

Edit: I ended up buying this card (msi rtx 4060 ventus 2x) and I'm running cyberpunk on low raytracing settings with a low of 80fps and a high of 120fps with dlss turned on with dlss off its much lower around 60fps to 80fps
I really like this card, it's low profile which is perfect for my mini build as I don't have a lot of desk space for a big case so I had to pick a smaller case/motherboard and obviously go for a smaller card which this fit the bill perfectly.

It's very power efficient and doesn't push my UPS too hard when it's running on its battery (which is important as I have brownouts/voltage fluctuations very often in my area).
This card doesn't get very hot either the hottest I've seen it is at 75c normally when gaming its sat at around 60-70c which is impressive compared to my old GTX card that would hit 80c to 85c when gaming (tbf that could be due to the lack of fans in my old build and also because its like a 2 year old card as apposed to the 4060 I've had for less than a month)
I will say that linus has some good points. 
This card isn't for everyone.
 If power consumption and size aren't a factor for you, then yeah, there are better options for about the same price.
However, for me, this is exactly what I wanted and needed, and I feel I made a really good choice picking this card up

I bought one.
It was in my budget and the power consumption was appealing to me.
Personally I don't game a lot but I use software for denoising RAW photos which is relatively GPU intensive. I also recently bought a new camera with a much higher resolution.
My previous 1660Ti would take about 50 seconds per image. In a worst case scenario, say a shoot after which I keep around 1000 images, processing all these shots would take about 13 *hours*. The 4060 would need about 3 to 4 hours for the same workload. While using less power than a 1660Ti. Saving me both time and money.
A 3070 would probably have been in the same price range, especially a used one, but it would have used more power. So I would have needed a new PSU as well and my PC would go beyond using 500 watts on full load. Which I simply don't *want*. 
It's my goal to have a PC that runs very efficiently. The 4060 fullfilled that role for me.

I get the anger from people who just want raw performance, but I think this isn't just about supporting Bitcoin miners or whatever you mentioned.
I think this is actually the long-term future whether you like it or not, because the main concerns moving forward in the realm of computing won't be solved by just guzzling more power to get more performance.
The main bottlenecks for advancement in computer tech now materially and socially are energy efficiency, heat production, and the fact that we've hit the limit for miniaturization of transistors without switching to non-electron computing (which also has considerations that bleed into the other issues).

While the 4060 and DLSS+frame gen might not be super appealing to people right now who just want raw power, this is clearly (at least in my opinion) about experimenting to find ways to move forward in a responsible way while looking at long-term goals.

I don't think it's the correct take to be so dismissive about these issues.

My past habits and patterns of buying graphics cards or computers used to be like this: For instance, about 10 years ago, I purchased a new graphics card for 1000. After buying it, I wouldn't bother keeping up with the latest news in the graphics card market; I would simply use it for 3-4 years. After 3-4 years, I would start to feel that the card is not performing well enough, struggling with many games. Then, I would think about buying a new card again, expecting that for the same price of 1000 , I should be able to get a card that is twice as powerful as the one I bought 4 years ago. Thus, I would make the purchase and indeed get a card with twice the performance.

However, this approach doesn't work anymore. A card that cost 1000， 4 years ago will only get me the same level of performance if I spend the same amount now. comments.text: I've said this in the past. Nvidia used RTX as a testing platform to real world test their RT cores for AI performance. What better to test AI by using RT cores to calculate light paths in real time. Once their concept for AI cores was proven a success they saw their chips weren't fast enough. So use those AI cores to run AI software to help upscale a lower resolution intelligently to improve ray tracing performance. Now 3 years in all this RTX bull crap has given all the real world evidence to sell their RT cores and AI servers to companies that would pay billions for it leaving gamers in the dust. I realized all this with the 3000 series and all the arguments over RTX and AMD can't compete in RTX, that i realized ray tracing was meaningless, especially when you can tell if it on or not due to the excellent work of the developer in lighting the scene. You see there are many people who still have not upgraded to an RTX card and so developers still have to do all the hard work lighting a scene correctly for those who don't use raytracing. The point of raytracing from Nvidia was you just light the scene then forget about it during development as the RT cores would handle all the work. Does really help developers when more than 60% of gamers are still using older cards. 4000 series now just shows that Nvidia was aiming for the AI business all along as that's where the billions of dollars are to be made and making graphics cards is small time business. They used their graphics card business to bench test their AI hardware for the AI market. Now they have the AI market they really don't need the graphics card market to lead their development of new hardware and gamers get left behind. comments.text:
A funny reminder that before the gpu shortage, generations of video cards just as little as 7-9 years ago, used to get up to 50-70% faster per generation like the 860 vs 960 vs 1060 vs 2060 era. Yes, that's right. 
You used to get 50-70% improvements PER generation while having the 60 series selling as a powerful card while only being 150-200$ for the base, 250$ for the ti/super version (vs 400$ today), and cards would regularly double the amount of vram they had before, from 2 gb 960 -> 3 gb 1060 -> 6 gb 2060 -> 12 gb 3060!

 Then in 2023, nvidia decided to release a card with 4 gb less vram (33-50% less than it's prodessor!), all while charging +50-100% than what the 150-200% cards had sold for before. 

If the 4060 had kept up with the trends of the past though, we'd likely have seen a 16 gb-20 gb 4060 sold for 200-250$, that would also have been 50-70% faster, outpacing even the ti edition and 500$ ram edition while likely costing 2x less. 

However there's no real point to rag over the lack of improvement post gpu mining boom. 

But nvidia is milking us for sure and the "silicon shortage" feels self regulated as their technology is higher than ever, yet they choose to dole less in order to maximize products and make sure your 500$ card expires in 2 years by cutting off the 12 gb -> 8 gb vram.

The chips would also be 20-40% faster as well, or even perform at the level of the series above them while sold at the same cost of the tier below. 

If that had kept up, you'd be able to get a 4070ti's current performance for the price of a 300$ 4060ti with 16-24 gb of vram.

The number would be a fantasy though, since they stopped giving such upgrades and now they're only 10% faster than last gen with less vram. 

However, the 200-260$ 12 gb 3060s and 3060tis have sold out now, so the price for performance is sadly mundane now that 3060's stock is dried up. 

And if you're spending 360$ for a 3060ti, and 380$ for a 10% faster 4060ti. You might as well just go the 4060ti. Not because it's a great price or improves upon the last gen much. (+10% is 10%). 

But just because eventually all the good prices got bought up. They still raised the price up in the 4000 generation 1 tier higher, without +1 tier performance of the past though.

comments.text:
I have always had a "meh" response to people claiming nvidia is better for gaming, it has ALWAYS been price to performance and power was never an object, neither was space, prettiness, and even hardware video encodes

heck I was on an athlon II x3 on am3, not am3+ until I finally saw ryzen 7 1700's drop through the floor, and yet I still got a dud chip once, 
but shout out to amd, all I had to do was report the BSOD code, do a tiny few messages of tag, ship out the old chip(not even the wraith spire RGB) and they send me a full retail replacement package with a spare spire RGb I gave to my bro for his 2000 series chip as he actually cared it was an RGB model, I never do

oh and even though I had a ton of fried NB chips on am3+ boards, that was entirely an issue with motherboard vendors not specifying you need forced fan flow over the chip, it was routinely at 95c (and thermally shutting off) at near-idle and not providing an easy way to mount a nice fan or including one, wasn't AMD's fault for motherboard vendors using whimpy thermal solutions for the main heat chip on a non-integrated CPU

so yeah, other than normal quirks of bad third-party design, a natural dud, and some driver growing pains(early win-10 had absolutely no basic USB drivers for ryzen and I had to learn I needed a new install image) I have always had luck with amd and their brands and the last intel chips I had were early core 2 duo chips, and it wasn't nice back in the P4 era either
I did have both a celeron and an intel P2 at one point and ironically I think I had better luck with the celeron(amd) PC back in my childhood, I still killed it with ESD as I used a staticy canvass bag to try and circumvent my parents "no computer" punishment but that was 100% a part of the era and entirely my fault
is nvidia often a few percent better, less than the increase in price? yes, is it worth that extra price when you are a casual gamer who doesn't care if he has to rock stable 30 instead of 60 fps and can't run over 1080p? absolutely not

so this is just another "fork you" nvidia is pushing on non-corporate users on top of so much else

"I encountered unfair treatment on my Sony PS5 console. I have a PS4 disc of COD13 (Infinite Warfare), and yesterday, while on the main menu of the game, I saw a remastered version of the original Modern Warfare in the bottom row (equivalent to additional content). I clicked on it and entered the PS5 store interface, which showed that I needed to purchase it. I didn't want to buy it, so when I tried to exit, I pressed the Circle O button (because it's the UI of the PS5 store interface). However, due to running the PS4 game, the O button directly became the confirm button (Sony's PS5 operation is X to confirm and O to cancel). It triggered my Alipay's payment without a password, and the purchase was successful. I immediately tried to get a refund when I returned to the game interface, and I never downloaded what I bought (the PS platform's refund policy is for digital content that has not been downloaded or used within 14 days of purchase).

First, Sony's technical problem caused a bug in the PS5 store's purchase interface, where the confirm and cancel buttons were reversed, leading to this erroneous payment without a password. Second, I am eligible for a refund because I never downloaded it, but they claimed that I had streamed and played the purchased content, even though I hadn't used the streaming function for a long time. Moreover, the reasons for the refusal of refund from the customer service and email were different. My old monitor was 2560x1080 75Hz and it handled it absolutely fine, still no problems if I dropped down to that res in a window for whatever reason.

1080p should never hit 60FPS at high/max settings unless a game is bumping up against its VRAM limit, or horrendously optimized (most Unity games or inexperienced UE4/5 devs).

I temporarily upgraded to a 3080 and it wasn't enough of an upgrade (~1.7x) because of the bus width/memory bandwidth (and 1G less) drop compared to the 1080 Ti; it did worse at higher resolutions than it should've. 3080 12G or 3080 Ti might've been fine, but nobody should've paid those prices.

In the end, I jumped to a 4090. 2x the MSRP for 4x the performance and major future proofing.  Very hard pill to swallow, but that's what we suffer sticking to a greedy corporation like NVIDIA.

If you're a 1080Ti owner and willing to go with AMD, get the 7900XTX and don't look back. No DLSS, but there's a DLSS2FSR mod out in the wild to mitigate this.

comments.text:
I'm still on my 3080 12GB, so far still performs well at 1440p.

My 'lack' of a 4K monitor helps, at 1440p I really don't need to jump on the RTX 4000 series, or the AMD cards either.

However, even if I did want to upgrade for some reason I wouldn't buy anything at current prices. Which leaves me in a situation where it's simply better to skip the current 'new' generation and wait for the next one. It's not the first time I do this. My previous card was a regular GTX 1080 (non-Ti) and it served me so well I simply skipped the RTX 2000 series entirely and eventually did make the move years later for my current 3080 12GB.

comments.text:
@nathangamble125  You're mistaking DLSS3 with frame generation. They're two separate things. Frame generation is supported by 40 series cards only right now and comes bundled with the DLSS3 integration into games. It doesn't need to be turned on and you can still benefit from DLSS3 itself (the deep-learning super sampling). DLSS3 also works on other nvidia cards that support DLSS. Just not the frame generation part.

DLSS2 is just version 2 of DLSS. DLSS3 is just version 3 of DLSS but with it is an addon which is Frame Generation. Like Path Tracing for example, you don't need to activate it but you can if you want. As for input lag, that only matters when it's highly competitive and the system is under heavy strain to provide baseline frames in the firstplace. If you're getting max 30 frames and need frame generation to provide 60 then you will definitely feel input lag. Nvidia provide a solution to reduce this but sometimes you have to compromise for quality as the player. If you don't want input lag, turn down your gfx settings to get more frame and use DLSS3 on its own.

There's always a compromise somewhere, and again I don't see any other company trying to push boundaries do you?

So basically, don't use frame generation for online competitive sports like counter-strike. But use frame generation if you're trying to max out cyberpunk2077 DLC with path tracing enabled and don't mind a bit of input lag.

I should note that I do know and disagree with the greedy business practices of Nvidia this past 3 years. I know they can be dicks sometimes but they make up for it in free software for people like me who need it. This past 3 years was a total piss take though. The price hiking was insane and doing nothing to prevent scalpers drove me mad.

comments.text:
For anyone wondering "there's no uplift, why does this card even exist?", you need to take a look at the die size. 4060's die is just a hair over HALF the size of the 3060's (146mm² vs 276mm²), making this card much cheaper to manufacture. Smaller die sizes have a huge effect on cost-per-die (since you can cram more of them onto a wafer) and also yields (since any lithography imperfections ruin a much smaller percentage of a wafer's overall chips)

Moore's Law isn't dead, NVIDIA has just decided that it should be the sole beneficiary.

i got a brand new 3070 ti for 400 dollars off ebay, founders.... took a risk, paid off. currently thats probably the best way to get a gpu for a decent price. the 8gb of vram is just not great for vr rendering at 5k, but many games can hit 90, like red matter 2 running max rendering at 6k for me , good90fps no issues. it looks amazing, running above native res does fill in the gaps and crisp up the image, its noticable where "jaggies" are concerned. even going from 5k to 6k because i had 30% headroom completely eliminates traces of jaggies (the bane of my vr existence). it becomes insanely clear. but im a stickler for clarity, i even notice it over lower framerate. jaggies are harsh on the eyes and i hate it, but with this in mind, good antialiasing plus running almost double resolution if i have the headroom is a pretty solid way to go, but it NEEDS good antialiasing, which i gotta say, many desktop game ports do not deliver. clarity is on a per game basis, so far red matter 2 is the most clear ive ever seen, right behind contractors at ultra aa, and kayak mirage. why buy a new card with less performance for more money like the 4060, when you can get a better last gen for cheaper. many people who play vrc say 3060 ti is better because 12gbs of vram, its not true, vram isnt everything, comparatively my friend who has a 3060 ti was still getting less performance at the same max settings in the same room, which was capping both of our vram. performance still trumps vram numbers in the end if the gap in performance metrics aside from that is large enough. although my frametimes were slightly worse, but thats not something youll notice when its somewhere in the ballpark of 10-15ms same cpu and ram speed/capacity. to anyone thinking this is a solution, DONT downgrade, youll be kicking yourself. im willing to sacrafice frames for clarity and resolution, but not graphics quality. i often find the 30 series just like most series struggles with shadows and volumetrics the most, these are the only real settings you need to seriously watch out for, aside from lod/distance rendering. i find vr to be a great way to force a system to its limits. also disable asw, its going to give you smoothness, but introduce a ton of performance issues, if you dont know, reprojection is not asw or motion smoothing. its why you rarely see it dip below 45, but its reprojecting, so its not really showing 45, its more like 72-90 depending, just might see ghosting if youre on a moving object like a boat or car when it turns, but not when you turn your head with asw off. youll get an objectively worse experience with asw unless you have motion sickness. reprojection is always on. you will immidiately notice if asw is on with snap turn, it smears every time you turn below a solid 90 with headroom.

vr is a great reason nvidia really needs to step up their game, its becoming very popular these past few years with covid. and making it look amazing FAR FAR outweighs desktop performance metrics they are aiming for. where dlss is concerned, we need something that can ADD it to unsupported games, like amds fsr, vr performance kit is a drop in dxgi file that works with any dx11 game, intended for vr, but can be used for any dx11 game, atleast unity and unreal. drop in the file, open the config file, and 1.0 is default, can change it to say 0.8 to get 20% performance back with minimal fidelity loss. very easy. not sure if this would even work, but something needs to change with nvidia, i had 8gbs of vram in 2015, shared memory is not ideal in all situations or games. native vr games get a TON of optimization we have been brainwashed to not expect in desktop games, thus ports running far worse than native games.

comments.text:
I don't totally understand the aversion to DLSS. At the end of the day, if my games are running better, that's the important thing, regardless of whether it's software or hardware responsible for it (and with DLSS it's kind of both because it's the Tensor cores specifically running the AI upscaling stuff). And DLSS 2.0 honestly looks better than turning the resolution down. I have a 4k monitor, and using DLSS quality mode at 4k looks a whole lot better than just turning my resolution down to 1440p and letting my monitor just blow that up to 4k without the benefit of DLSS. The latter looks blurry as hell, and the former is basically indistinguishable from native 4k unless you stop playing and sit there scrutinizing the pixels closely, and even then, in a double blind test, you'd be hard pressed to consistently guess which is which.

I guess the concern about Nvidia pushing DLSS so hard is that it'll lead them to not try to push their hardware game as hard? I mean okay sure, I get that. But at the same time, if DLSS can run games better for less energy cost, isn't that a good thing? How is this different from when rasterization was a new thing? Isn't that essentially just a rendering shortcut, as well? I won't profess to be an expert about any of this, but I just feel like people tend to have this irrational aversion to DLSS.

comments.text: DLSS is cool, my problem is that it needs per-game support, meaning that the vast majority of games out there does not and probably will not support it. And there's also an issue where they are locking software behind hardware. If a game you want to play comes out with a support for a newer version of DLSS than Nvidia allows on your GPU, then DLSS will simply not work for you. Meaning that using DLSS in performance benchmarks is hugely misleading, because whether you'll get that performance just depends on the circumstances of the game's release, and not on your hardware.

comments.text:
I just wanna speak up and give credit where it's due for DLSS improvements from the 30 series to 40 series as someone who recently upgraded from a 3060ti to a 4070ti for anyone interested in firsthand experiences from others. Just a note, though, I did get a better deal on the 4070ti by getting an open box model, but it was still new, for $200 off. And I was one of the people who ran my 3060ti at 4k. I'm less picky than most on what FPS is acceptable. As long as it's stable, I'm perfectly fine with as low as 45 FPS. (I know people will say that's blasphemous lol)

Now, for the DLSS stuff. I would use DLSS on my 3060ti when I needed to but I could always tell that it was on. The fidelity was always just suffering enough that it was noticeable. On the 4070ti, however, I started benchmarking several games, CP77 and Control being the ones I new took a lot of power to run at 4k high settings with RT on. When I first started CP77 I was super impressed at how much FPS I was getting and how stable it was on the 4070ti and it looked great, then I went to the settings to enable DLSS only to find that it was already on. This surprised me as I couldn't even tell the difference while messing around that it was on. That blew my mind as I was used to it being fairly obvious on the 3060ti. But that did mean I was already getting the FPS boost, which was significant. I was getting about 50-55 FPS on Ultra with RT on with DLSS, and that dropped to 30-35 with DLSS off, but considering the graphics stayed the same quality it's an easy choice to keep it on.

Frame generation, on the other hand, is still something I will opt to keep off until/unless the drivers get an update that really reduces latency. While it would be fine in slower paced games with little real-time action, in games like Control and CP77 the latency increase was just too much to play comfortably. It's right on that cusp of tolerable, but ultimately uncomfortable to play with.

I will say, though, that on CP77 they added a new RT mode called Path Tracing, which with nothing enabled reduces my FPS by half from the regular Ultra RT. (I'm talking 10 FPS to 5 FPS lol). But with both DLSS and Frame Gen enabled I was hitting my 45 FPS goal, but that introduced that latency.

All in all, I'm impressed with the software side of the 40 series stuff, it's just their MSRP that is really screwed up. But I'm glad I made the jump from my 3060ti to a $200 off 4070ti. As someone who games in 4k that boost to VRAM and the software will pay off for a few years of gaming, I think.

comments.text:
The main reason this keeps working out for nVidia is very simple: crypto miners. They are such a dominant part of the industry that they were the biggest source of energy consumption in the US last year. So nVidia knows there's going to be shortages, they know they can raise the price and they know they don't have to care because they will get sold anyway. So until the crypto scam industry collapses due to full regulation, this is going to be the unfortunate standard we continuously have to deal with.

Come to think of it I bet those are probably the only kind of people who would even be interested in a XX60' series card from nVidia in the first place.

With that said... it's a 40"60" RTX. And it's not a "Ti". You have to be crazy to expect it to compete with better nVidia series cards of last generation. It's a 4060 RTX, you get meh performance that is slightly better than the last generation's XX60 and because its new you still pay a new price.

Which brings me to the secondary reason: nVidia releasing cards out of order (e.g. great cards) who -- if you are lucky enough to find some that aren't sold out and have dropped a bit in price -- will become a more appealing option by the time you get a new generation's weaker cards. In fact there's very little point in even doing them anymore if you ask me.

Though with that said, I'm going to put my foot down and say you can still do worse than a budget nVidia card: an AMD card. Other than the outward appeal of price/performance on their budget lines of cards, there's no real incentive to get it. And a buddy of mine that got one recently proved to me that no, AMD still doesn't have stable drivers.

But yeah TL;DR the 4060 is bad, XX60 lines are always bad (e.g. you don't want to upgrade into it, ever, for any reason) and you shouldn't expect nVidia to put effort in their "budget" cards until the crypto industry is dead. And even then, "budget" cards are becoming absolutely pointless as more developers want to deliver their games in optimal quality only to reduce staff workload and improve overal presentation of their game... and... why would you want a budget card? To do not fully what you want a PC to do for your games and applications? Even for daily tasks you're starting to be better off of just doing that from your mobile device and hooking that up to your screen or consideirng a VM integration. Which is a good trend, because that allows the IT sector to start pushing users to devices catered and controlled for them while the advanced/power users can stick to the machines they need, really. Not sure how I got to that statement from a 4060, but there you go.

comments.text:
Most people (myself included on most days) have a very difficult time keeping things interesting for an extended period of time. Another important thing is understanding how much information is too much - and understanding how to break up huge information dumps into digestible pieces by interspacing with scene changes, questions, examples, and so forth - where by we allow the audience to take in what is going on, and then refocus on the next piece of information.

One of the easiest ways to ensure this is happening is to have multiple presenters and give them charge of certain aspects with a back and forth tag team appraoch. But both parties must be ready to give way to the other - and not over step in terms of how long they are blathering on or you end up in the same problem as before with the audience tuning out. In many ways - this is why News stations have Segments, or multiple news anchors do mini discussions on topics, and so on as it helps to create the environment of natural shifting and pausing necessary to hold attention, and give wider context.

And so: If you ever have to describe something, teach something, or plan to write something - just keep this in mind: Balance the amount of information, with the pacing of presentation - with pauses between major idea's. If you can master this, you can likely teach anything to anyone provided you are willing to sit down and learn a bit about it first.

comments.text:
TL;DW

- Based on the video, the RTX 4060 is not a good value for money card, as it performs worse than the last gen RTX 3060 Ti and AMD RX 6700 XT in most games, even with DLSS and frame gen enabled. The only advantage it has is its low power consumption and thermals, but that may not be enough to justify its price.
- The video also suggests that the AMD RX 6700 XT is the best bang for your buck card in this price range, as it offers much higher performance than the RTX 4060 and similar performance to the RTX 3060 Ti, while having more VRAM (12 GB vs 8 GB) and costing only $10 more at the time of writing.
- Some other inferences that can be made from the video are that Nvidia is not focusing on improving their hardware for mainstream gamers, but rather relying on software tricks like DLSS and frame gen to boost their performance. The video also implies that Nvidia is more interested in serving their AI customers than their gaming customers, as they have a higher profit margin and demand.
- Some of the sticking points about all of this are that Nvidia's RTX 40 series cards are overpriced, underpowered, and have limited availability due to chip shortages. The video also criticizes Nvidia for cutting down the number of cores, memory bandwidth, and PCIe lanes on their cards, which could affect their future performance and compatibility. The video also questions the usefulness of ray tracing on these cards, as it causes a significant drop in frame rate and is only supported by a few games.

comments.text:
Imagine selling a GPU for $300 that can't beat midrange cards from last year and still can't beat the PS5 or Xbox Series X performance wise. Even their last-gen 3060Ti beats it.

They're seriously betting on DLSS 3 and frame interpolation to bridge the gap, so they can get away with selling people a worse product. Like DLSS 3 isn't bad in practice, just that it's excused bad optimization on the developer's end and products that could be way better priced. Fake frames will always feel worse than real ones, this is just the sample and hold equivalent to black frame insertion, and there's still some issues regarding artifacts that need to be ironed out. $300 should NOT be a 1080p card, considering the 750Ti was sold as a 1080p card that traded blows with console performance back in 2014 and only costed $150, and same for the 1050Ti. They put about as much effort into this card as they have with their control panel or linux drivers over the past ten years. And that's before even getting to the fact that they refuse to open source the DKMS modules for older NVIDIA cards before the 20 series, and the fact that they cut out 3D Vision and Shield Streaming from their Windows drivers, really calling into question how long their still capable hardware will last for. Yay for more e-waste, buy the latest GPU even if it makes no financial sense, you will own nothing and be happy.

Maybe I was right for buying a 6700XT for $300, because I just wanted a Living Room PC build running SteamOS with none of the console subscription or closed wall nonsense, and none of the driver/controller/resolution nonsense associated with Windows. Raytracing is either going to be held back by consoles anyways or not always be worth the framerate impact. Like the stuff recently with Starfield is bad, but this still doesn't change the fact that NVIDIA shills always come out of the woodwork to rant about off-topic stuff simply to simp for a company that's singlehandedly killing PC Gaming (Setting aside Microsoft, because they do nothing outside of making Windows worse to use) at the expense of Valve and others that have built it up and would be within their best interest to keep it where it is (90-100M monthly concurrent users).

I'm hoping that Valve revives the Steam Machine concept, while offering console equivalent performance for cheap, otherwise PC gaming is dead.

comments.text:
To answer those arguing RTX4060 or Ti is "mid-range" when its 8GB VRAM is so limiting: 1080p even at ultra settings is NOT midrange in 2023! There are plenty of people who're playing at 4K ULTRA now (high end), so "mid-range" now would be 1440p ULTRA settings with playable FPS and no glitches! Logically this means that basic entry level (budget) gaming in 2023 STARTS at 1080p ULTRA settings with smooth FPS and zero glitches - a 8GB VRAM graphics card CANNOT manage that even with all CURRENT games, with upcoming games planning on needing even more VRAM!

An 8GB VRAM GPU in 2023 is a 720p card, which is a resolution and performance which was long in the tooth a decade ago and should be dead and buried before now! We need to move on and allow games companies to put "16GB VRAM" on the GPU for MINIMUM required specs to play the game without NVidia and AMD shortsightedly and greedily holding them back! Doubling VRAM from 8GB to 16GB only costs $20 more but makes a MASSIVE difference!

Another point: low VRAM is making MUCH bigger game installations (150GB not unusual) because it has to include crappy low resolution textures, as well as photorealistic textures for those with enough VRAM, to allow MIPMAPPING, which increases used drive space by a huge 33%! Aim for a GPU with 16GB VRAM or more, even if that means switching to AMD as high VRAM graphics makes a MUCH bigger difference than fake extra filler frames that cause latency by NVidia! 

DON'T pay over $199 for a GPU with 8GB VRAM, regardless of any other card tricks, because it's ALREADY e-waste and can't even handle all current games at 1080p ultra entry level!

comments.text:
I really dislike frame interpolation. It looks very bad IMO when you're trying to use frame interpolation to go from 30 to 60. It makes animation feel slippery and removes punch from animation. Mostly because frame interpolation doesn't handle information like acceleration and jerk. It might be acceptable to go from 60 to 120 but that's a bit niche IMO, since you're increasing latency for a game that's already at a decent framerate.

From what I know, there really isn't plans to add derivative information and such, though that could just increase latency even further if there isn't game support, and that game support is probably expensive to do as its adding additional rendertargets. So relying on frame interpolation will always result in excessively smooth animations with no weight.

If you like frame interpolation that's fine, but I don't think it's a substitute for real frames that accurately sample animation tracks, or real frames that respond to your input.

DLSS3 requires developer input to add those motion vectors as well, and my god are motion vectors annoying to program & debug. Granted most games these days do TAA so they've already paid that pain, but there's still DLSS3 integration time for a imo gross effect.

comments.text:
I'm confused. It beats the 3060 in every category, so why are we comparing to the 3060Ti? If it was aiming to beat the 3060 at a lower price, they accomplished that. Then you factor in RTX and DLSS and it goes above and beyond the 3060.

They obviously aren't trying to beat AMD price / performance in pure raster, but I don't think Nvidia was ever truly trying to. Nvidia has mostly, in recent times, been about the things around raster. RTX, gameworks, shadowplay, CUDA support in productivity apps, NVENC, physx, and the list goes on.

That won't be a justification for everyone in the market, but for my workflow it certainly is.

Ultimately this does feel reminiscent of Intel with 14nm, but nvidia is just putting out incremental updates to try and keep the product offering fresh enough, but they're almost certainly leaving themselves room to grow from here. I've heard rumors of 4000 series super, I wouldn't be surprised by that. But ultimately, it seems like every other generation or so, Nvidia does a bare minimum. Most of the market seems to upgrade on every pinnacle upgrade. 700 series, 1000 series, 3000 series, and I imagine 5000 series will show enough of a performance leap over 3000 for the market to shift to that next.


4000 series has value, but when you compare it to last gen or AMD on just pure raster alone, obviously it doesn't seem that exciting.

comments.text:
You know, this was very interesting. I could see it coming months ago, of course. But the comments the video made at the end REALLY resonated with me. I’m way past angry at Nvidia (and AMD) at this point, I just don’t care anymore. Earlier this month I decided PC gaming is just not worth the cost or the hassle anymore. I just bought myself a switch and will be playing that through the summer (to avoid the stupid amounts of heat my gaming PC outputs to my house, making my AC fire up even more often and longer, costing me money). I’ll keep my 3060 for the next 4 years or so, and relegate my gaming PC to occasional gaming sessions lowering resolution to 1080p. I'll just buy an M1 Mac Mini for YouTube/work which will sip power in comparison to my 5600/3060 just on desktop tasks. In 2027 if there's any non offensively priced GPU, I might upgrade my PC then (because I have 500+ Steam games and I'd hate losing access to 3 decades of my purchases, and I'm not really into the steam deck).

It’s been a great 25+ years, but I’m just done. The PC gaming industry doesn't make sense anymore, it's become abusive of the consumer. If you lived through the 90s and early 2000s you'd see that clear as day. Today, Nintendo makes fun games in a ridiculously small and energy efficient package. Apple makes their own silicon computers that consume 6x less power (bought an m1 MBA last year and I'm never looking back on energy efficiency, fans, heat output, and battery life). At this point in 2023, I’d rather spend my money on travel than yet another overpriced GPU that sounds like a plane engine and heats up my house with the heat of a thousand suns. No thank you.

comments.text:
@zereimu  That's fine, I don't agree with that, but I never said that this was a big issue. It's just an opinion I have. 

I think that the contrast between high production quality footage and low production quality production footage in the same video makes the low footage stick out more and look even worse. I would be fine with it just being low quality video. However, they have invested into good equipment and clearly value producing higher fidelity content. To that goal the low quality footage is a determent. As well as in this case it limited the presenters range of expression that they usually have. 

A lot of the time when you want to create something the important question is not how much can you add, but, how much can you remove. Why not is the wrong question, why should you is the correct one. Everything you ad should have a purpose in building what you want to create. Every decision you make should have a reason for being your best option. 

It's also professional to say, "Hay, I am not the best for this role at the moment. Someone else should take over."

But to be clear I am not condemning them for doing It. I just think it's an interesting topic, that's all. Edzel, Hoffmann, Andy, they all do great work and I'm sure they had great reasons for doing it this way. Even if I would disagree with it. I could be the one who is wrong about it. I don't recognize Adam's name but he wrote the script and this is how he wanted it. He did a very good job at the script clearly and might have just not been able to change it in time. Intelligent people made these decisions. But it's still fun to voice my own opinion on it in a constructive way. 

Anyways, best of luck to you. Hope you have a wonderful day.

comments.text:
Honestly even watching the dlss videos, a big part of where you want fps is to reduce input latency for a fps and aim better. On 30 fps, aiming for headshots is like trying to aim at a fly with a shotgun under stobelights that aims in intervals of 5 inch gaps frame to frame. On 120 fps, it's like aiming through butter.

The dlss problem is it seems to generate the fake frames while RAISING input latency that seems to defeat some points. A big major part of fps is gaming at ultra, but the generated frames when viewed at 1/10th speed seem heavily blurry low quality images. It looks a lot like that interpolating software used for 12 hand drawn fps to 60 interpolated fps animation. It looks fine in motion, but when taken frame for frame, it's just blurring the two frames together while adding input lag. 

Plus even in games you might want it, what's the point of spending 100-200$ for a feature that only generates fake frames on like 30 of 1000 games? It sounds handy for 4k, but if i mess with dlss on my nvidia card, at 1080p i find it makes things more blurry than just running native and the quality loss of running dlss is actually higher than the quality loss of going 8 gb on ultra textures to 4 gb vram on medium settings. 

The dlss blur gets fps sure, but it actively hurts everything i use fps for. Turning the camera introduces more motion blur (less reaction/clarity), movement looks worse, and the input lag added is counterintuitive for the reason i change fps. I chase fps so i can have a more reactive game, nvidia dlss chases fps AT EXPENSE of a more reactive game. 

DLSS sounds super handy for 4k upscaling but im not sure if a 100-200$ upcharge is worth it. 

The energy efficency is neat, but you'd have to basically run it 24/7 bitcoin mining or stable diffusion/ai running over 5 years at 24/7 use to break even. (10 years if underclocked for 70% performance at 45% power, for 160% power/watt efficiency. Which someone cared about high electric prices/heat probably would.). Yet graphic cards tend to have peers at 2x the strength for the same msrp come every 5-7 years. So by the time you broke even on electricity usage on normal 1-8 hr a day usage, the card could already be 5 years obsolete. 

It's a okay price if you want to buy new, but i got my 3060ti for 250$ vs 400$, and some people have even reported getting super deals from 40-180$ 1080tis or 12 gb vs 8 gb amd's with better price to performance AND 12 gb vram over 8. 

I'm locked to nvidia for ai/cuda/stable diffusion. (It runs 2-3x faster than amd at ai due to xformer optimizations only working for nvidia). But it's really hard to say that Nvidia's past track record of breaking the last gen's tier above with each gen seems broken. 

This is the first 060 series to have less vram than it's predessor (299$ for 8 gb 4060, vs 200-250$ for *12* gb 3060). The 3060ti 8 gb is 20% faster for 20% less (260$ used) than the 4060. It really looks like nvidia targeted this generation at miners with the 100$ surcharge for electricity usage, a smaller bus, and if they kept up their past tradition of surpassing a tier ahead, the card with these exact same specs and fps and performance of a 400$ 3060ti could have been this card sold as a 230$ 4050, with the new 4060ti matching the 20% faster 3070ti's performance while being sold for 300$ vs 400$. 

The 4060ti would be a 20% better card available for 30% less for 50% more bang per buck if it had held up to past generational standards.

comments.text:
@clouds5  Yeah exactly. It's not a bad feature, but buying performance based on generated frames is a really poor way to bring the lackluster bang for buck of the 4060s up. 

If they were true frames, or every generated frame came with trivial input delay and good enough crispness options to make them usable in fps shooters, it'd be a great comparison.

But when you actually own the pc, and play it, the quality decrease in movement and game response doesn't always feel great. A lot gets compressed out by youtube's 30-60 fps cap and compression. 

But anyone who's been in front of a pc knows, home render quality can often radically exceed youtube's capped quality. And you buy the card for your home experience. 

I only have a medium end card, but paying 40% more for a feature that only generates fake blurred images while adding input latency that's often unavailable on 90% of the games i play, just doesn't make sense for a +40-70% sticker price fee. 

Plus rumor or not, some people gossip amd sponsors games to have amd's fsr instead of dlss. And since fsr is compatable with both, you're paying a massive sticker fee for a feature you might not even use on 90% of your games. 

The 4000 series could be neat for 24/7 energy efficiency or new box prices. But there's a serious question if they're overpricing the cards while hiding the lack of bang per buck, using expensive blurry interpolation to optimize stockholder profits.

On the AMD side, you should go for the RX 6700 XT or RX 6750 XT. They are both rocking 12 GB at around $350.

The only NVIDIA cards worth buying right now are : 
- RTX 4070 12 GB, not the Ti one, around $600, so more than the AMD offering for 12 GB, but you gain better Ray Tracing, DLSS, and Frame Generation
- RTX 4090 from $1600 all the way to $2500, so around $2000, because it's simply the best!

Here you go, 350, 600, and 2000 bucks. The question you should ask yourself now, is which game you want to play, with which screen, when will you change screen, how future-proof you want the GPU to be, and do you think the experience of playing with the RX 6700 XT will change you that much in comparison to the RTX 4090?
